resources.string: Your estimated body clock matches %1$s time.
To adapt: %1$s with your plan, %2$s without one.
Chart of hours your body clock is off %1$s time. With your plan: %2$s at landing, in sync in %3$s. Without a plan, as a rough guide: %4$s at landing, %5$s.

%1$s is %2$s ahead. This plan shifts your body clock %3$s later. After a large eastward time change, morning light at the destination can delay your body clock. Most body clocks also run slightly longer than 24 hours, which can make later shifts easier. Researchers disagree on when to choose this direction.

%1$s is %2$s behind. This plan shifts your body clock %3$s earlier. This requires a larger total shift. For this trip, the planner estimates that its light and sleep timing supports this direction more reliably. Researchers disagree on when to choose this direction.
Adapting starts with your first pre-trip day.
No jet lag expected. Enjoy the trip.
%1$s and %2$s have nearly the same local time. Keep your usual sleep, %3$s to %4$s local time, and get some daylight in the morning.
Short trip: staying on home time
Your trip is too short for full adaptation. The plan keeps your sleep schedule on %1$s time where possible and uses light for alertness.
Your estimated body clock matches %1$s time.
Not medical advice. Healthy adults only; not for flight crew on duty.
In the air to %2$s, where it\'s %1$s and dark
In the air to %2$s, where it\'s %1$s and light
Tip: pinch out on the dial to see your route on the globe.
You can follow the next scheduled step. Recording a missed step does not change your schedule or recalculate the adaptation estimate.
Not medical advice. If you have a health condition, are pregnant or take medication, talk to a doctor before changing your sleep or using melatonin.
No plan steps are scheduled right now.
Light after your estimated body clock low point helps shift your clock earlier, as this plan requires.
Light before your estimated body clock low point helps shift your clock later, as this plan requires.
Light now could shift your body clock in the opposite direction to the plan. Reduce light during this window.
A small dose of melatonin in the afternoon or evening tells your body night is coming sooner, which moves the clock earlier.
Melatonin in the morning nudges your clock later. Keep the dose small.
This sleep window follows your estimated body clock. The planner limits how far bedtime can move from your usual bedtime in local time.
Sleeping at night at your destination helps your body clock adjust to local time.
Your trip is short, so the plan keeps your body clock on home time instead of moving it twice.
Caffeine can help you stay alert now. The plan stops suggesting it well before your next sleep, but its effects vary.
Caffeine lingers for hours. Skipping it now protects your next sleep.
You may feel less alert near your estimated body clock low point. Avoid driving if you feel sleepy.
A short nap can reduce sleepiness. Keep it short to limit its effect on your next sleep.
This is your scheduled flight. The plan includes light and sleep steps for your time in the air.
It\'s night for your body. If you can\'t sleep on planes, rest in the dark with an eye mask: darkness still helps the shift.
Go outside if you can. Daylight is usually brighter than indoor lighting, even on cloudy days. Indoors, sit near a window and turn lights on.
Avoid dim rooms. Ordinary daylight or bright indoor light is enough. No sunglasses.
Wear dark sunglasses, dim your screens and keep away from windows.
Keep the room cool, dark and quiet. An eye mask and earplugs can help. If you cannot sleep, rest in the dark.
Set an alarm. Keep the nap short to limit its effect on your next sleep.
Only if you\'re tired. Keep it short and set an alarm.
Take the type and dose you\'ve agreed with your doctor. Don\'t drive for a few hours afterwards.
Choose small amounts of coffee or tea during this window.
Switch to water, herbal tea or decaf until your next sleep.
Avoid driving if you feel sleepy. Rest or take a short walk if you can.
Follow the cards that run during the flight: they say when to sleep and when to keep the window shade up.
Based on the human phase response curve to light (Khalsa et al. 2003; St Hilaire et al. 2012).
Light on the wrong side of the phase response curve moves the clock the wrong way (Khalsa et al. 2003).
Based on the phase response curve to melatonin (Burgess et al. 2010).
Shifting sleep gradually around travel speeds up adaptation (Eastman & Burgess 2009).
For trips of a few days, staying on home time avoids two rounds of jet lag (Waterhouse et al. 2007).
Caffeine\'s half-life is 3–5 hours; caffeine even 6 hours before bed shortens sleep (Drake et al. 2013).
Alertness is lowest near the body temperature minimum (Dijk & Czeisler 1995).
Short naps relieve sleep pressure with little effect on the body clock (Lovato & Lack 2010).
Times come from your flight details, in each airport\'s local time.
Darkness at the right time protects the shift even without sleep (Eastman & Burgess 2009).
